article_title: Metacognitive monitoring of working memory performance and its relationship to academic achievement in Grade 4 children
citation: Freeman, Emily E.; Karayanidis, Frini; Chalmers, Kerry A. (2017). Metacognitive monitoring of working memory performance and its relationship to academic achievement in Grade 4 children. Learning and Individual Differences, Vol. 57. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.06.003
title: Working Memory Power Test for Children (WMPT)
description: The WMPT is a computer-administered test of children's working memory with five levels of increasing difficulty, from a Memorise condition to a 4-Swap condition requiring four position swaps. It is "unique in that it captures both accuracy and confidence information and thus provides an opportunity to measure metacognitive monitoring ability in children". After each item the child rates confidence on a 4-point scale from guessed to definitely right. The article reports the test has good reliability (.85).
requirements: Requires children to give a confidence rating on a 4-point scale after each item, enabling calculation of calibration measures
constraints: Developed by ebilities, a publisher and supplier of online cognitive ability tests; validity evidence cited as under review at the time
target_learners: Grade 4 primary school children (aged approximately 9-11 years)
examples: In the study, children completed 25 problems across five levels (Memorise, 1-Swap, 2-Swap, 3-Swap, 4-Swap) on a laptop computer during the school day
key_sources: Freeman, Emily E.; Karayanidis, Frini; Chalmers, Kerry A. (2017). Metacognitive monitoring of working memory performance and its relationship to academic achievement in Grade 4 children. Learning and Individual Differences, Vol. 57. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.06.003

article_title: Distinct influences of affective and cognitive factors on children’s non-verbal and verbal mathematical abilities
citation: Wu, S. S., Chen, L., Battista, C., Watts, A. K. S., Willcutt, E. G., & Menon, V. (2017). Distinct influences of affective and cognitive factors on children's non-verbal and verbal mathematical abilities. Cognition, 166, 118-129. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2017.05.016
title: Working-memory-centered mediation account of affective and cognitive influences on distinct math skill components
description: The article proposes that WM is the central hub through which affective (math anxiety) and attentional factors influence children's mathematics: math anxiety and attention problems reduce WM resources, which in turn support computation and problem solving. Its stated summary is that "WM is a domain-general ability pivotal to children's math performance on both non-verbal and verbal problems". The account distinguishes non-verbal NO, where effects are fully WM-mediated, from verbal MR, where math anxiety also acts directly and reading and attention contribute additional pathways.
requirements: Assessment of WM as a latent construct from multiple subtests (Counting Recall, Backward Digit Recall, Digit Recall, Block Recall), alongside math anxiety, attention, reading, and IQ measures
constraints: Cross-sectional data could not establish causal direction
Tested in a nonclinical sample of 2nd-3rd graders (mean age 8.34 years) with IQ above 80
target_learners: children in early elementary school (2nd-3rd grade)
examples: Structural equation modeling in 330 children selected the Full Mediation model for NO (44.1% variance) and a Partial Mediation model for MR (60.4% variance)
key_sources: Wu, S. S., Chen, L., Battista, C., Watts, A. K. S., Willcutt, E. G., & Menon, V. (2017). Distinct influences of affective and cognitive factors on children's non-verbal and verbal mathematical abilities. Cognition, 166, 118-129. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2017.05.016

article_title: Feature versus object in interpreting working memory capacity
citation: Wuji Lin, Chenxi Lv, Jiejie Liao, Yuan Hu, Yutong Liu & Jingyuan Lin. (2024). Feature versus object in interpreting working memory capacity. npj Science of Learning 9:67. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00279-x
title: Integration-before-storage account of visual working memory capacity
description: The article proposes that visual working memory does not allocate resources directly to each individual item but may integrate items to some extent before storage, yielding a non-linear complexity–capacity relationship. It draws on resource theory and Gestalt grouping, and cites work suggesting both feature-based and object-based storage may exist in WM, with retention format linked to task demands. As the authors put it, "it might integrate these items to some extent before storage."
requirements: Novel materials manipulating complexity within a single feature dimension (superposed lines) so that feature dimension and feature quantity are not confounded
constraints: The study was unable to quantify information across all dimensions or analyze the relationship between each dimension's information and WM capacity mathematically
target_learners: college students with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participating in visual working memory experiments
target_learning_goals: understanding the storage units and capacity limits of visual working memory
examples: Experiment 6 fitted a binary polynomial regression model relating complexity, number of items, and WM capacity, verified on a separate sample of 30 participants
key_sources: Wuji Lin, Chenxi Lv, Jiejie Liao, Yuan Hu, Yutong Liu & Jingyuan Lin. (2024). Feature versus object in interpreting working memory capacity. npj Science of Learning 9:67. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00279-x

article_title: Publisher Correction: Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant
citation: Yicong Zheng, Pengyuan Sun and Xiaonan L. Liu. (2023). Publisher Correction: Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant. npj Science of Learning (2023) 8:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00185-8
title: Working-memory-resource model of retrieval practice versus restudy distinguishing consumed resources from the extra cost of testing
description: The corrected Fig. 3 depicts a resource model comparing a Retrieval Attempt path with a Re-encoding path, each shown for High WM and Low WM, against a Restudy condition. It tracks Initial Episode Node Strength to Final Episode Node Strength, with "WM Capacity Available WM Resources Consumed WM (strengthen the node) Extra cost of test (no strengthening)" as annotated components. Retrieval and re-encoding consume working memory resources to strengthen the node, while testing carries an extra cost with no strengthening; restudy rows are marked N/A for these components.
requirements: Working memory capacity must be represented as available resources to model strengthening versus non-strengthening outcomes.
constraints: The supplied text presents this model only through the corrected figure's labels and axis annotations, without derivations or parameter values.
target_learners: learners studied in the original article on retrieval practice and working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied material as indexed by episode node strength
examples: The corrected figure contrasts Retrieval Attempt and Re-encoding panels, each split by High WM and Low WM, against a Restudy panel whose cost components are marked N/A.
key_sources: Yicong Zheng, Pengyuan Sun and Xiaonan L. Liu. (2023). Publisher Correction: Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant. npj Science of Learning (2023) 8:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00185-8

article_title: A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect
citation: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0
title: Working-memory-dependent dual-process model of the testing effect
description: The model posits that the testing effect comprises two temporally ordered processes: retrieval attempt, the initiation of a search for the answer, and post-retrieval re-encoding, the reiteration of the correct answer in working memory after successful retrieval. The article states that "the testing effect comprises two processes: retrieval-attempt and post-retrieval re-encoding". Both processes draw from the same pool of working memory resources, enabling a trade-off between WM expenditure and memory fortification, which explains why people with different working memory capacities benefit differently from testing.
requirements: Working memory resources available during the task, linked to individual WMC and the WM demands of the material
constraints: The evidence that both processes consume the same WM pool remains indirect; direct empirical validation is still lacking, per the article
target_learners: learners varying in working memory capacity
examples: The model was first introduced by Zheng et al. to explain individual differences in the testing effect, with behavioral evidence from image-word pair learning
key_sources: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0

article_title: The Effects of Mathematics Strategy Instruction for Children with Serious Problem-Solving Difficulties
citation: Swanson, H. L., Orosco, M. J., & Lussier, C. M. (2014). The Effects of Mathematics Strategy Instruction for Children With Serious Problem-Solving Difficulties. Exceptional Children, 80(2), 149-168. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Working memory resource demands as a precondition for successful strategy training
description: The article frames strategy effectiveness through cognitive load theory, whose "centraltenet isthat instruction shouldbe designedinalignmentwith thelearner's cognitivearchitecture,which consistsofa limited- capacityworkingme mory system." It hypothesizes that "theavailability of ampleworking memory resourcesisan important preconditionforstrategytrainingtobe successful," because children with smaller WMC may be overtaxed by certain strategies. The combined verbal+visual condition is interpreted via Mayer's hypothesis that combining verbal and visual resources places fewer demands on WMC. The study tests competing models (basic skills, general resource, high cognitive skills, compensatory) against WMC–outcome correlations.
requirements: Strategy instruction must be matched to learners' working memory capacity; ample WMC resources are posited as a precondition for success
constraints: The authors state WMC would not be the only processing variable accounting for outcomes, and effects might differ when children with both computation and reading difficulties are included
target_learners: Grade 3 children at risk for math difficulties in problem solving
key_sources: Swanson, H. L., Orosco, M. J., & Lussier, C. M. (2014). The Effects of Mathematics Strategy Instruction for Children With Serious Problem-Solving Difficulties. Exceptional Children, 80(2), 149-168. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1048482

article_title: Cognitive Strategies, Working Memory, and Growth in Word Problem Solving in Children with Math Difficulties
citation: Swanson, H. L., Lussier, C. M., & Orosco, M. J. (2013). Cognitive Strategies, Working Memory, and Growth in Word Problem Solving in Children With Math Difficulties. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 48(4), 339–358. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219413498771
title: Working memory as a limited-capacity processing resource underlying strategy effectiveness in mathematical problem solving
description: The article defines working memory as "a processing resource of limited capacity, involved in the preservation of information while simultaneously processing the same or other information." It hypothesizes that ample WM resources are "an important precondition for strategy training to be successful for children with MD," because strategies rely on declarative representations and serial processes that require large amounts of WMC, and newly acquired strategies impose demands on WMC.
requirements: Learners must have sufficient spare WM resources to benefit from cognitive strategies
constraints: Children with MD are known to experience WM difficulties, limiting spare capacity for strategy use
examples: Word problem solving requires accessing prestored information, accessing the appropriate algorithm, and applying problem solving processes to control execution while ignoring irrelevant information
key_sources: Swanson, H. L., Lussier, C. M., & Orosco, M. J. (2013). Cognitive Strategies, Working Memory, and Growth in Word Problem Solving in Children With Math Difficulties. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 48(4), 339–358. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219413498771

article_title: Computer-assisted instruction versus inquiry-based learning: The importance of working memory capacity.
citation: Chevalère Johann, Cazenave Loreleï, Berthon Mickaël, Martinez Ruben, Mazenod Vincent, Borion Marie-Claude, Pailler Delphine, Rocher Nicolas, Cadet Rémi, Lenne Catherine, Maïonchi-Pino Norbert, Huguet Pascal. (2021). Computer-assisted instruction versus inquiry-based learning: The importance of working memory capacity. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0259664
title: Working memory demands account for the differential effectiveness of CAI and IBL
description: The article proposes that the CAI advantage and its WM moderation reflect differences in cognitive load imposed by each instructional design. Because content was identical across conditions, the authors interpret the interaction as a consequence of instructional design: CAI's navigational nature, hypertext links and autonomy tools may distract attention and raise extraneous cognitive load, so higher-WM students benefit more. Conversely, IBL's collaborative structure may distribute memory across partners: through transactive memory, "each partner works as a memory aid for the others", reducing individual WM demands. The significant interaction is taken to indicate CAI imposes greater WM demands.
requirements: Content held identical across methods so effects can be attributed to instructional design
Teachers trained to provide appropriate guidance levels, which reduces cognitive load in IBL
constraints: The article states it could not determine exactly which characteristics of CAI specifically tap into WM
The account is the authors' interpretation, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: Science and Technology knowledge (Physics-Chemistry, Earth and Life Sciences, Technology)
examples: The authors explain the interaction via CAI's navigational demands on extraneous load and via transactive memory distributing load across IBL group members
key_sources: Chevalère Johann, Cazenave Loreleï, Berthon Mickaël, Martinez Ruben, Mazenod Vincent, Borion Marie-Claude, Pailler Delphine, Rocher Nicolas, Cadet Rémi, Lenne Catherine, Maïonchi-Pino Norbert, Huguet Pascal. (2021). Computer-assisted instruction versus inquiry-based learning: The importance of working memory capacity. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0259664
